_about: The Coach's numbers and reasons, from docs/coach-proposal.md (approved 2026-10-14). The engine reads every threshold from here, so tuning one never means touching logic. Each rule's principle is what the Why? button shows, with its sources.

A1.name: Finding your weight
A1.principle: Rating how many reps you had left is a practical way to set the weight, so the first sessions start light and let each set's rating pick the next one. People tend to underestimate what's left by about a rep, which is why calibration aims a rep softer.

A2.name: Double progression
A2.principle: Reps climb inside a range; once you own the top of it, the weight goes up and the reps reset. It's the most reliable way to keep adding challenge without guessing.

A3.name: Too easy: move faster
A3.principle: When every set lands at the top with plenty left, one small step would still be easy, so the weight jumps to what should land mid-range. Jumps stay within about 10% for newer lifters, in line with the classic 2–10% guidance.

A4.name: Missed reps
A4.principle: For size, muscle grows across a wide range of weights as long as the sets are hard, so a slightly lighter weight with every set in range wins. For strength, the heavy weight itself is the stimulus, so the weight stays and the rep target drops a notch.

A5.name: Big equipment jumps
A5.principle: When the next weight on a machine is a big jump, adding reps first works too: progressing reps builds muscle about as well as progressing load, and the weight range for growth is wide.

B1.name: Harder than expected
B1.principle: Adjusting the weight from how hard sets feel works about as well as fixed percentages, so a set that came out much harder than planned resets the rest to a weight that lands in range.

B2.name: Easier than expected
B2.principle: A set at the top of the range with lots left means the planned weight is light today. One step up keeps the remaining sets close to the target effort.

B3.name: Rest
B3.principle: Longer rests preserve reps across sets, and on heavy compound lifts around 2–3 minutes beats short rests for strength and size.

C1.name: Lower readiness
C1.principle: Short sleep lowers performance by about 8% on average, and how you feel tracks training stress well. A lighter day is offered, never forced.

C2.name: Very low readiness
C2.principle: On a really rough day, a short session of the key lifts keeps strength and the habit going at a fraction of the fatigue.

D.name: Plateaus
D.principle: When the same stimulus stops working, a planned change usually restarts progress: a lighter week if fatigue is the cause, a new rep range, or a close variation. Size and strength respond across many rep ranges, so a change costs little.

E1.name: Weekly sets
E1.principle: Muscle growth rises with weekly hard sets, roughly 10 or more per muscle, with diminishing returns near 20. Counting sets per muscle keeps every muscle in a productive band.

E3.name: Push and pull balance
E3.principle: Lifters who push much more than they pull often show shoulder strength imbalances. The link to shoulder problems is an association, not proven cause, so this is a low-priority suggestion.

F2.name: Lighter weeks
F2.principle: A planned lighter week (fewer sets, lighter, easy effort) clears fatigue. Lifters report doing one about every 5–6 weeks; a full week off can cost strength, so it's lighter, not off.

G1.name: Missed sessions
G1.principle: Training each muscle at least twice a week matters more than the exact day, so a missed session can move rather than disappear.

G2.name: Short on time
G2.principle: Keeping the big multi-joint lifts and pairing accessories as supersets roughly halves session time at similar volume.

G3.name: Coming back
G3.principle: Strength fades first after a break and comes back fast: in one study, ten weeks off were made up in about five. Easing in costs almost nothing and avoids a week of soreness.

G4.name: Consistency
G4.principle: Progress comes from weeks stacked on weeks. A missed week is a restart, not a failure.

H3.name: Fat loss
H3.principle: In a calorie deficit strength is largely kept while muscle gains slow. Losing about 0.5–1% of body weight a week best protects muscle; keeping the weights heavy is what holds on to it.

H3P.name: Protein
H3P.principle: Gains from extra protein level off around 1.6 g per kg of body weight a day. Atlas doesn't track food; this is a once-a-month pointer.

J1.name: Pain
J1.principle: Training through an injury can make it worse. A lift that hurts gets swapped or lightened, and symptoms that persist deserve a professional's look.

T.name: Technique
T.principle: Cues come from each exercise's own form notes. One cue at a time, rotated so the same one doesn't come back for a month.

K.name: Records
K.principle: Estimated max uses the Epley formula with the reps you actually did; it's most accurate up to about 10 reps.
